What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 would require anyone voting in person in California to present a government-issued ID, and those voting by mail ballot to include the last four digits of the government-issued ID number they provided when they registered to vote.
In-person voters without ID would be turned away, while mail ballots without an attached ID number that matches their registration would be rejected. Critics note the measure does not explicitly require election officials to reach out to voters to correct or “cure” a ballot that is missing an ID number before rejecting it, as they are required to do when a voter’s ballot signature does not match what’s on file.
The measure also would require the state to provide free voter ID cards to eligible voters upon request, and state and county election officials to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters using government data and publicly report the findings of that work.
Advertisement
Under current law, Californians are required to provide identification when registering to vote and must swear under penalty of perjury — a felony — that they are eligible to vote and a U.S. citizen. They must sign their mail ballots, and their signature is compared to the one the state has on file to verify their identity. It is already against the law for noncitizens to vote.
Proposition 39’s provisions echo but are less onerous than those proposed in the SAVE America Act (https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2026-03-14/republican-bill-poses-burden-for-many-u-s-voters), the strict voter ID and proof of citizenship measure Trump is pushing in Congress.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated Proposition 39 would “increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars.”

Luckey is the mother of billionaire tech entrepreneur Palmer Luckey (https://www.latimes.com/la-influential/story/2024-06-30/palmer-luckey-anduril), a major Trump fundraiser and Republican donor and the co-founder of Anduril, which manufactures autonomous weapons systems and recently won a $363-million contract (https://www.anduril.com/news/anduril-and-u-s-customs-and-border-protection-expand-partnership-with-200-additional-extended-range-sentry-towers) with U.S. Customs and Border Protection for hundreds of autonomous surveillance towers along the southern border.

# What to know about California's Proposition 39 ahead of general election
## What recent polls have found for Proposition 39
Recent polling on Proposition 39 has shown mixed results since September, with some surveys finding majority opposition and others showing a narrow lead for the voter ID measure.
An Independent Voter Project survey released Oct. 5 found likely voters favored the initiative 43% to 40%.
A SurveyUSA poll released Sept. 21 also found support for the measure, with 48% of likely voters backing it and 38% opposed.
Other polls have shown the measure trailing.
A Berkeley IGS survey released Sept. 25 found Proposition 39 failing by a 13-point margin, 52% to 39%, while a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Sept. 15 found 55% opposed and 43% in favor.

**This measure (2026 California Prop 39):**
- A constitutional amendment, submitted by Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego) / Reform California / Californians for Voter ID (the group's director is Julie Luckey, Palmer Luckey's mother)
- Funded by Richard Uihlein ($17M), Trump-aligned mega-donors; Yes side raised over $24–33M
- Requirements:
  - In-person voting: must present a government-issued ID every time
  - Mail-in voting: must write the last 4 digits of the chosen government-issued ID number on the return envelope; if it doesn't match the registration record, the ballot is invalidated. According to the LA Times, the measure does not clearly require a "cure" (correction) process for ballots missing an ID number
  - Free state-issued voter ID card upon request
  - Election officials must use government data to verify the citizenship of registered voters through "best efforts," and annually publicly report county-by-county percentages
  - State Auditor conducts a compliance audit in odd-numbered years
  - Requires the legislature to implement; many details left undefined
- Fiscal impact: Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year

**Opposition:** Governor Newsom, Senator Padilla, Nancy Pelosi, California Democratic Party, ACLU, Common Cause, League of Women Voters, labor unions. The Democratic establishment is strongly opposed.

**Polling:** Mixed, but the most recent high-quality data (Berkeley IGS, October 19–25, 2026) shows No leading Yes 57% to 37%. September IGS: 52% to 39% No. August: 51% to 42% No. However, some polls (SurveyUSA, Independent Voter Project, Mason-Dixon) show Yes leading or it's close. The most recent (October 19–25) Berkeley IGS poll shows a 20-point No lead. Note: IGS polls are widely regarded as high-quality. Also, among independents 54% voted No (August poll), which is noteworthy because the Yes side claims bipartisan support.

**Research on voter ID and turnout:** Mixed. GAO 2014: mixed findings; GAO analysis suggests voter ID caused turnout to drop 1.9–3.9 points in Kansas and 2.2–3.2 points in Tennessee (2008–2012). Other studies (NBER 2020, QJE 2021 "Strict ID Laws Don't Stop Voters") find no significant effect. The MIT Election Lab says the debate is ongoing. So the research is genuinely mixed, but much of the evidence suggests the effect on overall turnout is small; the risk to vulnerable groups (the poor, rural, those with name changes, the elderly) is a real but small concern in the context of California's all-mail system.

- California already verifies voter identity at the time of registration (DMV data, driver's license number / last 4 of SSN). So the marginal value of requiring ID at the time of voting is small in terms of fraud prevention.

- The mail-in ballot component (last 4 digits on the envelope) could create new invalid-ballot problems. In the last election, over 100,000 ballots were rejected for signature mismatch (per the Yes side's argument). Actually, in 2021 Texas changed its rules so that mail-in ballots are rejected if the return envelope is missing a voter registration ID number (the "voter's registration number"). Texas 2022: many more ballots were rejected. The "12 times more" claim is from the No side's rebuttal. Let's not rely on this too heavily.

- Prop 102 (1998) passed: required in-person registration with ID.
- Prop 203 (2004) "Voter Identification Initiative" — required ID for in-person voting and a free ID card; failed (about 42%).
- Prop 210 (2004) — "Voting by Mail" — required mail-in ballots to be…? Also, among independents 54% voted No (August poll), which is noteworthy because the Yes side claims bipartisan support.

**Research on voter ID and turnout:** Mixed. GAO 2014: mixed findings; GAO analysis suggests voter ID caused turnout to drop 1.9–3.9 points in Kansas and 2.2–3.2 points in Tennessee (2008–2012). Other studies (NBER 2020, QJE 2021 "Strict ID Laws Don't Stop Voters") find no significant effect. The MIT Election Lab says the debate is ongoing. So the research is genuinely mixed, but much of the evidence suggests the effect on overall turnout is small; the risk to vulnerable groups (the poor, rural, those with name changes, the elderly) is a real but small concern in the context of California's all-mail system.

**Context important for this measure:**
- California already verifies voter identity at the time of registration (DMV data, driver's license number / last 4 of SSN). So the marginal value of requiring ID at the time of voting is small in terms of fraud prevention.
- Voter fraud is extremely rare (the Brennan Center and others document single-digit cases).
- The citizenship verification component is a new one: annual county-by-county public reporting of the percentage of verified citizens. This is unusual; opponents argue it could be used to target voters; there is no evidence that non-citizen voting is widespread.
- The mail-in ballot component (last 4 digits on the envelope) could create new invalid-ballot problems. In the last election, over 100,000 ballots were rejected for signature mismatch (per the Yes side's argument). Adding another matching requirement with no explicit cure process (per the LA Times) could increase the number of rejected ballots.
- The claim that "Texas threw out 12 times more mail ballots" — Texas requires ID for in-person voting, but… actually, in 2022 did Texas require the last 4 of SSN on the mail-in ballot return envelope? No — that's not right. Did Texas's SB 1 (2021) require an ID number on the mail-in ballot return envelope? Actually, in 2021 Texas changed its rules so that mail-in ballots are rejected if the return envelope is missing a voter registration ID number (the "voter's registration number"). Texas 2022: many more ballots were rejected. The "12 times more" claim is from the No side's rebuttal. Let's not rely on this too heavily.

- Cost: Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year, with little proven benefit.

**Past history in California:**
- Prop 102 (1998) passed: required in-person registration with ID.
- Prop 203 (2004) "Voter Identification Initiative" — required ID for in-person voting and a free ID card; failed (about 42%).
- Prop 210 (2004) — "Voting by Mail" — required mail-in ballots to be…? No. Let me check: Prop 210 (2004) was "An act to amend the California Constitution to require that voters provide identifying information when voting by mail" or something like that? I'm not 100% confident. Let me search for the history.

Also worth checking: the Wikipedia page on the 2026 Prop 39 — has an overview, and includes a "Criticism" section, signature verification, and court rulings. Let me fetch that.

Also, let me read the rest of the LA Times article (offset 20000) to check the opposition section and other details (e.g., what the free ID card would look like, the citizenship verification mechanism, expert opinions).

And to check: what do independent election experts (e.g., Secretary of State Shirley Weber, election law scholars) say? And details on the citizenship verification provision — for example, how do "best efforts" using government data work (DHS/DLAA data?), and concerns about it (e.g., could it lead to removal of lawful voters?).

1. web_fetch the Wikipedia page for 2026 California Prop 39
2. web_fetch LA Times article with offset 20000
3. web_search "Prop 39 California citizenship verification best efforts"
4. web_search "Prop 203 2004 California voter ID failed"

Then, I may search for expert opinions (e.g., "election experts Prop 39 California opinion").

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 is opposed by leading state Democrats, major civil rights organizations including the American Civil Liberties Union and major labor unions in the state, who say the measure would disenfranchise eligible voters and expose voters to identity theft by forcing them to write personal ID numbers on mail ballot envelopes.
According to campaign finance reports, the ACLU of Northern California has contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars to defeating the measure. Quinn Delaney, a major Democratic donor and fundraiser for former President Obama, and Patty Quillin, a major philanthropist and wife of Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, both have given $1.5 million.
The Service Employees International Union Local 2015, which represents long-term caregivers, provided $1 million, the SEIU California State Council for Working People gave $500,000, and the California Teachers Assn., through its independent expenditure committee, gave another $500,000.
Arnulfo De La Cruz, president of SEIU California and SEIU Local 2015, said in a statement that the group’s members “know our nation is stronger when working people make their voices heard and have their ballots counted,” and that strict voter ID laws “are part of Trump and MAGA extremists’ agenda to rig the election system so they can cling onto their own power and get richer from corporate corruption.”
Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) recently convened a news conference where a slate of Democratic leaders — including state Senate President Pro Tempore Monique Limón (D-Goleta) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Hollister) — called on Californians to vote no on Proposition 39.

The Democrats called the measure a “dirty trick” from “Trump acolytes” akin to historic poll taxes designed to disenfranchise Black voters, and a power grab that would seriously harm millions of eligible voters, especially in Black and Latino communities.
“Proposition 39 is a direct assault on everything California stands for. Our people, our values and our fundamental belief that every eligible voter here in California deserves to have their voice heard and deserves to have their vote counted,” Rivas said.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Trump and his allies have for years claimed widespread fraud in U.S. elections, particularly in big blue states such as California. After his return to the White House last year, Trump began a fresh crusade (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-23/will-trump-interfere-in-midterms-democrats-their-allies-are-preparing) to rewrite election laws across the country.
Courts have rejected those efforts repeatedly, including on the grounds that the president does not have authority over elections. Backers of Proposition 39, including DeMaio, have been pushing for voter reform for years (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-03-02/voter-id-appears-headed-for-californias-november-ballot-what-you-should-know), but the effort gained steam this year as frustration with the limits on Trump’s executive power over elections mounted among his supporters.
DeMaio has said that the measure is badly needed to disrupt fraud and address plummeting public trust in elections. Padilla has said it is being pushed solely because “Donald Trump is scared” of his party losing power.

On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment.

Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 is opposed by leading state Democrats, major civil rights organizations including the American Civil Liberties Union and major labor unions in the state, who say the measure would disenfranchise eligible voters and expose voters to identity theft by forcing them to write personal ID numbers on mail ballot envelopes.
According to campaign finance reports, the ACLU of Northern California has contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars to defeating the measure. Quinn Delaney, a major Democratic donor and fundraiser for former President Obama, and Patty Quillin, a major philanthropist and wife of Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, both have given $1.5 million.
The Service Employees International Union Local 2015, which represents long-term caregivers, provided $1 million, the SEIU California State Council for Working People gave $500,000, and the California Teachers Assn., through its independent expenditure committee, gave another $500,000.
Arnulfo De La Cruz, president of SEIU California and SEIU Local 2015, said in a statement that the group’s members “know our nation is stronger when working people make their voices heard and have their ballots counted,” and that strict voter ID laws “are part of Trump and MAGA extremists’ agenda to rig the election system so they can cling onto their own power and get richer from corporate corruption.”
Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) recently convened a news conference where a slate of Democratic leaders — including state Senate President Pro Tempore Monique Limón (D-Goleta) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Hollister) — called on Californians to vote no on Proposition 39.
Advertisement
The Democrats called the measure a “dirty trick” from “Trump acolytes” akin to historic poll taxes designed to disenfranchise Black voters, and a power grab that would seriously harm millions of eligible voters, especially in Black and Latino communities.
“Proposition 39 is a direct assault on everything California stands for. Our people, our values and our fundamental belief that every eligible voter here in California deserves to have their voice heard and deserves to have their vote counted,” Rivas said.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Trump and his allies have for years claimed widespread fraud in U.S. elections, particularly in big blue states such as California. After his return to the White House last year, Trump began a fresh crusade (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-23/will-trump-interfere-in-midterms-democrats-their-allies-are-preparing) to rewrite election laws across the country.
Courts have rejected those efforts repeatedly, including on the grounds that the president does not have authority over elections. Backers of Proposition 39, including DeMaio, have been pushing for voter reform for years (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-03-02/voter-id-appears-headed-for-californias-november-ballot-what-you-should-know), but the effort gained steam this year as frustration with the limits on Trump’s executive power over elections mounted among his supporters.
DeMaio has said that the measure is badly needed to disrupt fraud and address plummeting public trust in elections. Padilla has said it is being pushed solely because “Donald Trump is scared” of his party losing power.

Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 is opposed by leading state Democrats, major civil rights organizations including the American Civil Liberties Union and major labor unions in the state, who say the measure would disenfranchise eligible voters and expose voters to identity theft by forcing them to write personal ID numbers on mail ballot envelopes.
According to campaign finance reports, the ACLU of Northern California has contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars to defeating the measure. Quinn Delaney, a major Democratic donor and fundraiser for former President Obama, and Patty Quillin, a major philanthropist and wife of Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, both have given $1.5 million.
The Service Employees International Union Local 2015, which represents long-term caregivers, provided $1 million, the SEIU California State Council for Working People gave $500,000, and the California Teachers Assn., through its independent expenditure committee, gave another $500,000.
Arnulfo De La Cruz, president of SEIU California and SEIU Local 2015, said in a statement that the group’s members “know our nation is stronger when working people make their voices heard and have their ballots counted,” and that strict voter ID laws “are part of Trump and MAGA extremists’ agenda to rig the election system so they can cling onto their own power and get richer from corporate corruption.”
Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) recently convened a news conference where a slate of Democratic leaders — including state Senate President Pro Tempore Monique Limón (D-Goleta) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Hollister) — called on Californians to vote no on Proposition 39.
Advertisement
The Democrats called the measure a “dirty trick” from “Trump acolytes” akin to historic poll taxes designed to disenfranchise Black voters, and a power grab that would seriously harm millions of eligible voters, especially in Black and Latino communities.
“Proposition 39 is a direct assault on everything California stands for. Our people, our values and our fundamental belief that every eligible voter here in California deserves to have their voice heard and deserves to have their vote counted,” Rivas said.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Trump and his allies have for years claimed widespread fraud in U.S. elections, particularly in big blue states such as California. After his return to the White House last year, Trump began a fresh crusade (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-23/will-trump-interfere-in-midterms-democrats-their-allies-are-preparing) to rewrite election laws across the country.
Courts have rejected those efforts repeatedly, including on the grounds that the president does not have authority over elections. Backers of Proposition 39, including DeMaio, have been pushing for voter reform for years (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-03-02/voter-id-appears-headed-for-californias-november-ballot-what-you-should-know), but the effort gained steam this year as frustration with the limits on Trump’s executive power over elections mounted among his supporters.
DeMaio has said that the measure is badly needed to disrupt fraud and address plummeting public trust in elections. Padilla has said it is being pushed solely because “Donald Trump is scared” of his party losing power.

On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment.

The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions.
On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.
Proposition 39 would establish new identification and citizenship-verification requirements for California elections.
State and local election officials would be required to make “best efforts,” using government records, to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually on the percentage verified in each county.

- History of California Initiatives: Initiatives by Title and Summary Year (PDF) (1912-): tabulation of proposed initiative measures that reached title and summary stage, including whether qualified for the ballot, and if so whether approved

Great progress. The main findings so far:

**This measure (2026 California Prop 39):**
- A constitutional amendment, submitted by Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego) / Reform California / Californians for Voter ID (the group's director is Julie Luckey, Palmer Luckey's mother)
- Funded by Richard Uihlein ($17M), Trump-aligned mega-donors; Yes side raised over $24–33M
- Requirements:
  - In-person voting: must present a government-issued ID every time
  - Mail-in voting: must write the last 4 digits of the chosen government-issued ID number on the return envelope; if it doesn't match the registration record, the ballot is invalidated. According to the LA Times, the measure does not clearly require a "cure" (correction) process for ballots missing an ID number
  - Free state-issued voter ID card upon request
  - Election officials must use government data to verify the citizenship of registered voters through "best efforts," and annually publicly report county-by-county percentages
  - State Auditor conducts a compliance audit in odd-numbered years
  - Requires the legislature to implement; many details left undefined
- Fiscal impact: Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year

**Opposition:** Governor Newsom, Senator Padilla, Nancy Pelosi, California Democratic Party, ACLU, Common Cause, League of Women Voters, labor unions. The Democratic establishment is strongly opposed.

**Polling:** Mixed, but the most recent high-quality data (Berkeley IGS, October 19–25, 2026) shows No leading Yes 57% to 37%. September IGS: 52% to 39% No. August: 51% to 42% No. However, some polls (SurveyUSA, Independent Voter Project, Mason-Dixon) show Yes leading or it's close. The most recent (October 19–25) Berkeley IGS poll shows a 20-point No lead. Note: IGS polls are widely regarded as high-quality. Also, among independents 54% voted No (August poll), which is noteworthy because the Yes side claims bipartisan support.

**Research on voter ID and turnout:** Mixed. GAO 2014: mixed findings; GAO analysis suggests voter ID caused turnout to drop 1.9–3.9 points in Kansas and 2.2–3.2 points in Tennessee (2008–2012). Other studies (NBER 2020, QJE 2021 "Strict ID Laws Don't Stop Voters") find no significant effect. The MIT Election Lab says the debate is ongoing. So the research is genuinely mixed, but much of the evidence suggests the effect on overall turnout is small; the risk to vulnerable groups (the poor, rural, those with name changes, the elderly) is a real but small concern in the context of California's all-mail system.

**Context important for this measure:**
- California already verifies voter identity at the time of registration (DMV data, driver's license number / last 4 of SSN). So the marginal value of requiring ID at the time of voting is small in terms of fraud prevention.
- Voter fraud is extremely rare (the Brennan Center and others document single-digit cases).
- The citizenship verification component is a new one: annual county-by-county public reporting of the percentage of verified citizens. This is unusual; opponents argue it could be used to target voters; there is no evidence that non-citizen voting is widespread.
- The mail-in ballot component (last 4 digits on the envelope) could create new invalid-ballot problems. In the last election, over 100,000 ballots were rejected for signature mismatch (per the Yes side's argument). Adding another matching requirement with no explicit cure process (per the LA Times) could increase the number of rejected ballots.
- The claim that "Texas threw out 12 times more mail ballots" — Texas requires ID for in-person voting, but… actually, in 2022 did Texas require the last 4 of SSN on the mail-in ballot return envelope? No — that's not right. Did Texas's SB 1 (2021) require an ID number on the mail-in ballot return envelope? Actually, in 2021 Texas changed its rules so that mail-in ballots are rejected if the return envelope is missing a voter registration ID number (the "voter's registration number"). Texas 2022: many more ballots were rejected. The "12 times more" claim is from the No side's rebuttal. Let's not rely on this too heavily.

- Cost: Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year, with little proven benefit.

**Past history in California:**
- Prop 102 (1998) passed: required in-person registration with ID.
- Prop 203 (2004) "Voter Identification Initiative" — required ID for in-person voting and a free ID card; failed (about 42%).
- Prop 210 (2004) — "Voting by Mail" — required mail-in ballots to be…? No. Let me check: Prop 210 (2004) was "An act to amend the California Constitution to require that voters provide identifying information when voting by mail" or something like that? I'm not 100% confident. Let me search for the history.

Also worth checking: the Wikipedia page on the 2026 Prop 39 — has an overview, and includes a "Criticism" section, signature verification, and court rulings. Let me fetch that.

Also, let me read the rest of the LA Times article (offset 20000) to check the opposition section and other details (e.g., what the free ID card would look like, the citizenship verification mechanism, expert opinions).

And to check: what do independent election experts (e.g., Secretary of State Shirley Weber, election law scholars) say? And details on the citizenship verification provision — for example, how do "best efforts" using government data work (DHS/DLAA data?), and concerns about it (e.g., could it lead to removal of lawful voters?).

Let me run these in parallel:
1. web_fetch the Wikipedia page for 2026 California Prop 39
2. web_fetch LA Times article with offset 20000
3. web_search "Prop 39 California citizenship verification best efforts"
4. web_search "Prop 203 2004 California voter ID failed"

Then, I may search for expert opinions (e.g., "election experts Prop 39 California opinion").

Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 is opposed by leading state Democrats, major civil rights organizations including the American Civil Liberties Union and major labor unions in the state, who say the measure would disenfranchise eligible voters and expose voters to identity theft by forcing them to write personal ID numbers on mail ballot envelopes.
According to campaign finance reports, the ACLU of Northern California has contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars to defeating the measure. Quinn Delaney, a major Democratic donor and fundraiser for former President Obama, and Patty Quillin, a major philanthropist and wife of Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, both have given $1.5 million.
The Service Employees International Union Local 2015, which represents long-term caregivers, provided $1 million, the SEIU California State Council for Working People gave $500,000, and the California Teachers Assn., through its independent expenditure committee, gave another $500,000.
Arnulfo De La Cruz, president of SEIU California and SEIU Local 2015, said in a statement that the group’s members “know our nation is stronger when working people make their voices heard and have their ballots counted,” and that strict voter ID laws “are part of Trump and MAGA extremists’ agenda to rig the election system so they can cling onto their own power and get richer from corporate corruption.”
Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) recently convened a news conference where a slate of Democratic leaders — including state Senate President Pro Tempore Monique Limón (D-Goleta) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Hollister) — called on Californians to vote no on Proposition 39.
Advertisement
The Democrats called the measure a “dirty trick” from “Trump acolytes” akin to historic poll taxes designed to disenfranchise Black voters, and a power grab that would seriously harm millions of eligible voters, especially in Black and Latino communities.
“Proposition 39 is a direct assault on everything California stands for. Our people, our values and our fundamental belief that every eligible voter here in California deserves to have their voice heard and deserves to have their vote counted,” Rivas said.
Why is this on the ballot?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Trump and his allies have for years claimed widespread fraud in U.S. elections, particularly in big blue states such as California. After his return to the White House last year, Trump began a fresh crusade (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-23/will-trump-interfere-in-midterms-democrats-their-allies-are-preparing) to rewrite election laws across the country.
Courts have rejected those efforts repeatedly, including on the grounds that the president does not have authority over elections. Backers of Proposition 39, including DeMaio, have been pushing for voter reform for years (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-03-02/voter-id-appears-headed-for-californias-november-ballot-what-you-should-know), but the effort gained steam this year as frustration with the limits on Trump’s executive power over elections mounted among his supporters.
DeMaio has said that the measure is badly needed to disrupt fraud and address plummeting public trust in elections. Padilla has said it is being pushed solely because “Donald Trump is scared” of his party losing power.

1. EDITORIAL: We asked the No on Prop. 39 campaign why voters should reject the measure
https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-39-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office, would require election officials to verify Californians' U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID.
...
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans' currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump's unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters.
...
39 offers no evidence that it makes elections safer, and a court held that imposing this "extra step" on voters certainly doesn't make voting easier.
...
Citizenship is already required for federal, state and almost all California local elections.

# The Sustainable Groundwater Management Act
In 2014, the California State Legislature adopted the historic Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), which established a statewide framework to protect groundwater resources.
...
## Why Do We Need SGMA?
SGMA was enacted to halt the unsustainable use of groundwater and bring groundwater basins into balanced levels of pumping and recharge.
Overuse and excessive groundwater pumping can overdraft aquifers, emptying them faster than natural systems can recharge them leading to: lowering of groundwater levels, permanent loss of storage in aquifers, land surface sinking (subsidence), degradation of water quality, seawater mixing with fresh groundwater in coastal areas (seawater intrusion), and diminished surface water supplies where surface water and groundwater are interconnected.
...
## What is SGMA?
SGMA is California's plan to help communities manage their groundwater for the long term.
SGMA requires local agencies to form groundwater sustainability agencies (GSAs) in high- and medium-priority basins, and develop and implement groundwater sustainability plans (GSPs).
- GSPs address overuse and excessive groundwater pumping and outline how GSAs will manage groundwater to achieve long-term sustainability without causing undesirable results (the significant and unreasonable effects associated with the six sustainability indicators listed above in the "Why Do We Need SGMA?" section).
- GSAs develop and implement GSPs.

# Statewide Groundwater Management
Groundwater basins act as a drought buffer  – or savings account – by providing available water when surface water supplies are low such as in dry or drought years.
In California, groundwater is used for drinking water in homes, used to support businesses, as well as farms and ranches where it is used to irrigate crops and provide water for livestock.
Groundwater refers to water stored below the Earth's surface in aquifers, which include porous layers of sand, soils and clay that holds water.
Stacked layers of aquifers make up a groundwater basin.
For decades, groundwater in some parts of the State has been pumped out faster than can be recharged, causing record low groundwater levels in those areas.
The State and locals are taking great strides to protect our groundwater resources for long-term use, so that groundwater basins can withstand varying changes in climate and continue to serve as a drought buffer in future years.

- Implementing the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA)

# Groundwater in California
## Groundwater is a vital, but threatened, component of California’s water supply.
- On average, groundwater basins provide approximately 40% of the water used by California’s farms and communities, and significantly more in dry years.
...
- In some basins, groundwater pumping has exceeded replenishment for decades, causing groundwater depletion or “overdraft.”

39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration.
Invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter’s registration (e.g., if voter designates Social Security number for registration, but provides driver’s license number on envelope, their ballot would not count).
Prohibits voting in person without presenting government-issued identification.
Requires elections officials to annually report percentage of each county’s voters whose citizenship status they have verified.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State’s website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter’s identity is established through the registration process by using their driver’s license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government- Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter’s identity when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
FISCAL EFFECTS
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote—for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS
Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.
PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID
Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.
Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.
California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.
VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION
Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.
PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION
Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.
YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID
Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.
In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.
Margit Whitlock , Democratic Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Tafa Jefferson , Republican Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Joe Green , Independent Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 brings the national debate (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-04-02/democracy-at-risk-california-needs-new-voting-protections-poll-shows) around U.S. election integrity home to California by proposing stricter new voter ID requirements for state elections — mandating that voters present government identification every time they vote in person, or cite a specific government ID number when voting by mail.
The measure is backed by prominent California Republicans and ultrawealthy supporters of President Trump, who is pushing even more onerous voter ID measures at the national level (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-23/will-trump-interfere-in-midterms-democrats-their-allies-are-preparing). The measure’s backers say it is necessary to prevent voter fraud and block noncitizens from casting ballots. They contend, without evidence, that such problems are widespread in California.
The measure is opposed by the state’s Democratic establishment and prominent civil rights groups, who say it will disenfranchise many eligible voters, particularly those of color, who are poor or live in rural communities, or who move often or have changed their names. They say the latter group would include many married women.
Advertisement
The opponents also contend — as do many independent election experts — that California already has robust measures for verifying the eligibility and identity of voters, and that voter fraud, including by noncitizens, is exceedingly rare.
A poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and co-sponsored by The Times (https://igs.berkeley.edu/research/berkeley-igs-poll) last year found that most Californians support (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-05-09/la-times-igs-poll-on-elections-and-voter-id) the idea of requiring a government ID every time a voter casts a ballot. A more recent Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt2d964377/qt2d964377.pdf) found that when voters were given the added context that supporters say the measure is necessary to prevent fraud and opponents say it could disenfranchise eligible voters, they were much more split (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-04-24/assemblymember-carl-demaios-ballot-measure-will-be-considered-by-voters-in-november).

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 would require anyone voting in person in California to present a government-issued ID, and those voting by mail ballot to include the last four digits of the government-issued ID number they provided when they registered to vote.
In-person voters without ID would be turned away, while mail ballots without an attached ID number that matches their registration would be rejected. Critics note the measure does not explicitly require election officials to reach out to voters to correct or “cure” a ballot that is missing an ID number before rejecting it, as they are required to do when a voter’s ballot signature does not match what’s on file.
The measure also would require the state to provide free voter ID cards to eligible voters upon request, and state and county election officials to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters using government data and publicly report the findings of that work.
Advertisement
Under current law, Californians are required to provide identification when registering to vote and must swear under penalty of perjury — a felony — that they are eligible to vote and a U.S. citizen. They must sign their mail ballots, and their signature is compared to the one the state has on file to verify their identity. It is already against the law for noncitizens to vote.
Proposition 39’s provisions echo but are less onerous than those proposed in the SAVE America Act (https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2026-03-14/republican-bill-poses-burden-for-many-u-s-voters), the strict voter ID and proof of citizenship measure Trump is pushing in Congress.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated Proposition 39 would “increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars.”

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 is supported by leading state Republicans and backed by major Republican and Trump donors.
Advertisement
The campaign to collect signatures and get the measure onto the ballot was led by Julie Luckey, director of the group Californians for Voter ID, who has insisted that it is “not a Republican or Democratic issue,” but “common-sense policy.”
Luckey is the mother of billionaire tech entrepreneur Palmer Luckey (https://www.latimes.com/la-influential/story/2024-06-30/palmer-luckey-anduril), a major Trump fundraiser and Republican donor and the co-founder of Anduril, which manufactures autonomous weapons systems and recently won a $363-million contract (https://www.anduril.com/news/anduril-and-u-s-customs-and-border-protection-expand-partnership-with-200-additional-extended-range-sentry-towers) with U.S. Customs and Border Protection for hundreds of autonomous surveillance towers along the southern border.
According to campaign finance reports, Californians for Voter ID has been bankrolled by other Trump megadonors as well, including Richard Uihlein (https://www.forbes.com/sites/siladityaray/2024/10/16/billionaire-dick-uihlein-poured-nearly-49-million-into-pro-trump-pac-filings-show/), chief executive of the shipping and packing supplies company Uline, who has given the campaign $17 million.

content.thinking:
Great progress. The main findings so far:

**This measure (2026 California Prop 39):**
- A constitutional amendment, submitted by Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego) / Reform California / Californians for Voter ID (the group's director is Julie Luckey, Palmer Luckey's mother)
- Funded by Richard Uihlein ($17M), Trump-aligned mega-donors; Yes side raised over $24–33M
- Requirements:
  - In-person voting: must present a government-issued ID every time
  - Mail-in voting: must write the last 4 digits of the chosen government-issued ID number on the return envelope; if it doesn't match the registration record, the ballot is invalidated. According to the LA Times, the measure does not clearly require a "cure" (correction) process for ballots missing an ID number
  - Free state-issued voter ID card upon request
  - Election officials must use government data to verify the citizenship of registered voters through "best efforts," and annually publicly report county-by-county percentages
  - State Auditor conducts a compliance audit in odd-numbered years
  - Requires the legislature to implement; many details left undefined
- Fiscal impact: Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year

**Opposition:** Governor Newsom, Senator Padilla, Nancy Pelosi, California Democratic Party, ACLU, Common Cause, League of Women Voters, labor unions. The Democratic establishment is strongly opposed.

**Polling:** Mixed, but the most recent high-quality data (Berkeley IGS, October 19–25, 2026) shows No leading Yes 57% to 37%. September IGS: 52% to 39% No. August: 51% to 42% No. However, some polls (SurveyUSA, Independent Voter Project, Mason-Dixon) show Yes leading or it's close. The most recent (October 19–25) Berkeley IGS poll shows a 20-point No lead. Note: IGS polls are widely regarded as high-quality. Also, among independents 54% voted No (August poll), which is noteworthy because the Yes side claims bipartisan support.

**Research on voter ID and turnout:** Mixed. GAO 2014: mixed findings; GAO analysis suggests voter ID caused turnout to drop 1.9–3.9 points in Kansas and 2.2–3.2 points in Tennessee (2008–2012). Other studies (NBER 2020, QJE 2021 "Strict ID Laws Don't Stop Voters") find no significant effect. The MIT Election Lab says the debate is ongoing. So the research is genuinely mixed, but much of the evidence suggests the effect on overall turnout is small; the risk to vulnerable groups (the poor, rural, those with name changes, the elderly) is a real but small concern in the context of California's all-mail system.

**Context important for this measure:**
- California already verifies voter identity at the time of registration (DMV data, driver's license number / last 4 of SSN). So the marginal value of requiring ID at the time of voting is small in terms of fraud prevention.
- Voter fraud is extremely rare (the Brennan Center and others document single-digit cases).
- The citizenship verification component is a new one: annual county-by-county public reporting of the percentage of verified citizens. This is unusual; opponents argue it could be used to target voters; there is no evidence that non-citizen voting is widespread.
- The mail-in ballot component (last 4 digits on the envelope) could create new invalid-ballot problems. In the last election, over 100,000 ballots were rejected for signature mismatch (per the Yes side's argument). Adding another matching requirement with no explicit cure process (per the LA Times) could increase the number of rejected ballots.
- The claim that "Texas threw out 12 times more mail ballots" — Texas requires ID for in-person voting, but… actually, in 2022 did Texas require the last 4 of SSN on the mail-in ballot return envelope? No — that's not right. Did Texas's SB 1 (2021) require an ID number on the mail-in ballot return envelope? Actually, in 2021 Texas changed its rules so that mail-in ballots are rejected if the return envelope is missing a voter registration ID number (the "voter's registration number"). Texas 2022: many more ballots were rejected. The "12 times more" claim is from the No side's rebuttal. Let's not rely on this too heavily.

- Cost: Tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars per year, with little proven benefit.

**Past history in California:**
- Prop 102 (1998) passed: required in-person registration with ID.
- Prop 203 (2004) "Voter Identification Initiative" — required ID for in-person voting and a free ID card; failed (about 42%).
- Prop 210 (2004) — "Voting by Mail" — required mail-in ballots to be…? No. Let me check: Prop 210 (2004) was "An act to amend the California Constitution to require that voters provide identifying information when voting by mail" or something like that? Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 is opposed by leading state Democrats, major civil rights organizations including the American Civil Liberties Union and major labor unions in the state, who say the measure would disenfranchise eligible voters and expose voters to identity theft by forcing them to write personal ID numbers on mail ballot envelopes.
According to campaign finance reports, the ACLU of Northern California has contributed hundreds of thousands of dollars to defeating the measure. Quinn Delaney, a major Democratic donor and fundraiser for former President Obama, and Patty Quillin, a major philanthropist and wife of Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, both have given $1.5 million.
The Service Employees International Union Local 2015, which represents long-term caregivers, provided $1 million, the SEIU California State Council for Working People gave $500,000, and the California Teachers Assn., through its independent expenditure committee, gave another $500,000.
Arnulfo De La Cruz, president of SEIU California and SEIU Local 2015, said in a statement that the group’s members “know our nation is stronger when working people make their voices heard and have their ballots counted,” and that strict voter ID laws “are part of Trump and MAGA extremists’ agenda to rig the election system so they can cling onto their own power and get richer from corporate corruption.”
Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) recently convened a news conference where a slate of Democratic leaders — including state Senate President Pro Tempore Monique Limón (D-Goleta) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Hollister) — called on Californians to vote no on Proposition 39.

The Democrats called the measure a “dirty trick” from “Trump acolytes” akin to historic poll taxes designed to disenfranchise Black voters, and a power grab that would seriously harm millions of eligible voters, especially in Black and Latino communities.
“Proposition 39 is a direct assault on everything California stands for. Our people, our values and our fundamental belief that every eligible voter here in California deserves to have their voice heard and deserves to have their vote counted,” Rivas said.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Trump and his allies have for years claimed widespread fraud in U.S. elections, particularly in big blue states such as California. Courts have rejected those efforts repeatedly, including on the grounds that the president does not have authority over elections. ## Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
### Summary
On July 27, 2026, Californians for Voter ID filed a lawsuit against the Secretary of State challenging the new ballot title for Proposition 39, which was drafted by Attorney General Rob Bonta after his office received the amendment.
The plaintiffs argued that the new title of “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification,” was false and misleading, as it did not include the original title’s reference to additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements.
The Attorney General’s Office maintained that the revised language more accurately describes the measure’s provisions.
On August 6, 2026, Sacramento County Superior Court found for the state and ruled that the ballot title is sufficient, thus the measure will remain on the ballot unchanged.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.

The state would provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one. What barriers would remain for eligible voters?
Even if the voter ID card is free, plenty of hurdles remain. People still have to take time off work, arrange transportation and childcare, gather paperwork or pay fees to get copies of documents like birth certificates and deal with bureaucracy. For anyone with mobility issues, a tight schedule, limited financial resources or trouble accessing government offices, these steps can go from inconveniences, to challenges, and then become real barriers — and all to satisfy disproven election conspiracies. In short, just because something is free doesn’t mean it’s easy or accessible for everyone. Requiring the state to issue IDs just for voting, when our elections are already secure, pushes underrepresented voters further out of democracy and wastes a massive amount of taxpayer money.
In-person voters currently identify themselves by signing the voter roster, but the LAO says those signatures generally are not verified before ballots are counted. Is that adequate?
California already has a safe and accessible process to check that someone is registered and eligible to vote at the polls. Election officials verify the identity and eligibility of everyone in the voter registration database and regularly maintain and update those records using reliable sources, including DMV and Social Security records. Requiring in-person voters who have already been verified to provide name, address and a signature swearing under penalty of law that they are who they say they are ensures security without creating new barriers. The real question is whether adding another ID requirement would actually make our elections more secure, or just make it harder for people to vote. Prop. 39 offers no evidence that it makes elections safer, and a court held (https://www.courthousenews.com/california-judge-rules-voter-id-supporters-must-rewrite-ballot-arguments/) that imposing this “extra step” on voters certainly doesn’t make voting easier.
Evidence indicates that in-person impersonation is extremely rare. Does its rarity mean no additional precaution is warranted, even in an election decided by one or two votes?
We should only add new rules if they address an actual problem and the benefits outweigh the downsides for eligible voters. The conservative Heritage Foundation found (https://www.businessinsider.com/voter-election-fraud-statistics-rare-president-biden-trump-2020-2020-11) that between 2000 and 2020, out of 250 million votes cast by mail in the U.S., there were only 193 proven fraud cases. The Brennan Center also found that in-person voter impersonation is so rare that someone is more likely to be struck by lightning. These numbers show that our elections are already secure. Prop. 39 isn’t a precaution — it’s unnecessary and adds expensive bureaucratic barriers that could block millions of eligible Californians from voting. The twin goals of elections should always be expanding access to increase participation for eligible citizens and ensuring the will of the voter though secure and accurate procedures. We have the second goal covered in California; we should focus more on the first one.
Heritage’s database does not establish a fraud rate, but it documents proven election offenses. Which documented vulnerabilities do you believe California’s current system has not adequately addressed?
Every state, including California, has had rare and isolated cases of election misconduct, and those should be, and are, taken seriously. But a handful of cases — out of hundreds of millions of votes — doesn’t mean there’s a big flaw in the system. It means the system is working effectively to keep the number so dramatically low. California already has strong, well-researched and tested processes to keep voter rolls up to date, check registration information, prevent double voting or impersonation and audit ballots. If Prop. 39 is supposed to solve a real problem, that problem needs to be clearly defined and backed by evidence that current safeguards aren’t enough. Otherwise, it only creates new barriers for eligible voters, which compounds the real problem of low and unequal turnout by eligible voters in our democracy.
California currently verifies mail-ballot signatures. What is your objection to adding a match of four identification digits, assuming eligible voters receive notice and an opportunity to correct mistakes?

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.

The state would provide a voter ID card at no cost to voters who request one. What barriers would remain for eligible voters?
Even if the voter ID card is free, plenty of hurdles remain. People still have to take time off work, arrange transportation and childcare, gather paperwork or pay fees to get copies of documents like birth certificates and deal with bureaucracy. For anyone with mobility issues, a tight schedule, limited financial resources or trouble accessing government offices, these steps can go from inconveniences, to challenges, and then become real barriers — and all to satisfy disproven election conspiracies. Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.

PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 2:52 PM PST | UPDATED: November 3, 2026 at 4:43 AM PST

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 39, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026), would require election officials to verify Californians’ U.S. citizenship and prohibit them from voting without a government-issued ID. It also creates other rules around the voting process and identity verification when voting in person vs. by mail and ongoing compliance checks.
Voting “yes” would mean that you need to present a government-issued ID to vote in person and if you’re voting by mail, you need to provide the last four digits of that ID.
Voting “no” means the process stays is it is — you don’t need to present an ID to vote and your citizenship is verified during the registration process.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Voter Identification, Citizenship Verification, and Registered Voter List Administration Initiative, see it as a common-sense solution to voter fraud and a way to boost confidence in our elections.
Opponents see it as an extension of the Republicans’ currently stalled SAVE America Act and Donald Trump’s unfounded assertion that he lost the 2020 election thanks to noncitizen voters. It is also seen as a way to reduce voter participation by making it harder to vote.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://wp.me/p7ShJJ-SXLk).
How many eligible Californians do you expect Prop. 39 would prevent from voting, and what evidence supports that?
No one knows exactly how many eligible Californians Prop. 39 would block from voting, but we know that extra, unnecessary ID requirements don’t affect everyone equally. In other states, similar rules have led to eligible voters having their ballots rejected because of missing, incorrect or mismatched ID info. When Texas rolled out similar mail-ballot ID rules, mail ballot rejections shot up to 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) and the Brennan Center for Justice found that Black, Latino and Asian voters had their ballots rejected at higher rates than white voters for ID mistakes or omissions. Recent studies, including from the University of Maryland (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/pubs/Voter%20ID%20survey%20Key%20Results%20June%202024.pdf), have also shown that Californians are significantly less likely to have a current ID if they are people of color, younger, lower-income or have a disability. When eligible voters are turned away or their valid ballots are rejected, they’re less likely to try to participate in future elections.
